abstract: Fish respond to sound through behavioural changes, but whether these responses are associated with individual differences in emergence behaviour remains unclear. We examined emergence behaviour across two successive tests and its association with immediate responses to sound in 112 adult zebrafish (Danio rerio). Emergence latency was used to classify fish as bold, intermediate, or shy. Latency to enter the upper half of the aquarium was measured before treatment onset, while vertical midline crossings were quantified during 20-s windows immediately before and after sound or ambient-treatment onset. Emergence latency decreased significantly in the second test, and individual latencies were weakly positively correlated across tests. Upper-half latency did not differ significantly between bold and shy fish. Changes in midline crossings differed significantly between treatments, with a greater reduction under sound exposure than under ambient conditions. Exploratory analyses provided insufficient evidence that the association between emergence latency and changes in crossings differed between treatments for either emergence test. These findings demonstrate individual variation and changes in emergence behaviour across successive assessments, alongside an immediate effect of sound on vertical movement. However, they do not establish stable personality differences or emergence latency as a predictor of sound-specific behavioural responses.
